content.text:
Prompt Interpretation: You’re asking me to make an evidence-based case that Keir Starmer values human rights. I interpret “prove” here as: identify clear, verifiable actions, policies, and statements that reasonably indicate a commitment to human-rights norms, while acknowledging counter-evidence.

Reasoning Process: I can’t disclose my private step-by-step chain-of-thought, but here’s the concise approach I used:
- Define evaluation criteria: adherence to human-rights frameworks (e.g., ECHR/HRA), concrete legislative/executive actions affecting rights, professional track record in rights work, and responses to current rights controversies.
- Gather recent, reputable sources (BBC, Reuters, GOV.UK, major newspapers, legal/professional records).
- Test evidence against criteria across multiple domains (migration/asylum, labour rights, equality/anti-discrimination, free expression/press, foreign policy).
- Note counter-evidence and weigh it against the record.

Assumptions:
- “Values human rights” means maintaining core human-rights architecture (e.g., ECHR) and taking material steps that protect or advance rights, even if balanced with other policy aims like border control.
- Public, on-the-record actions and legislation are better indicators than slogans.
- The most relevant horizon is up to today (October 2, 2025), so recency matters.

Final Answer:
On balance, there is strong, verifiable evidence that Keir Starmer values human rights, shown by long-standing professional engagement with rights, explicit commitments to international human-rights frameworks, and several domestic measures that protect rights—tempered by a more restrictive turn on aspects of asylum policy in late 2025.

What supports the claim
- Sustained commitment to the ECHR and rule-of-law framing:
  - As Prime Minister, Starmer has repeatedly ruled out the UK leaving the European Convention on Human Rights; in November 2024 he stated “We will never withdraw from the ECHR,” and in PMQs on September 3, 2025, he called withdrawal a “profound mistake,” while signalling a review of certain interpretations (not abandonment) of provisions like Article 8. ([politics.co.uk](https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2024/11/04/we-will-never-withdraw-from-the-echr-keir-starmers-interpol-general-assembly-speech/?utm_source=openai))
- Reversal of policies criticised as curbing rights at work:
  - His government moved to repeal the Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Act 2023 and advanced an Employment Rights Bill expanding worker protections—clear steps aligned with freedom of association and labour rights. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/public-services-back-on-track-as-strikes-act-to-be-repealed?utm_source=openai))
- Protection of the core asylum law framework while ending Rwanda offshoring:
  - On July 6, 2024, he confirmed the Rwanda deportation scheme was “dead and buried,” replacing it with an enforcement-led approach targeting smuggling gangs—keeping removals within legal limits rather than using offshoring criticised by rights groups. ([bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))
- Equality and anti-discrimination agenda:
  - Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledged to remain in the ECHR, enact the Equality Act’s socio‑economic duty, and pursue race-equality measures—policy moves typically viewed as strengthening rights protections. ([bihr.org.uk](https://www.bihr.org.uk/get-informed/legislation-explainers/uk-general-election-2024-manifestos-and-human-rights-what-do-they-say?utm_source=openai))
- Record on tackling antisemitism and protecting minorities:
  - He took high-profile actions against antisemitism within Labour and, as PM on October 2, 2025, pledged to protect the Jewish community after a Manchester synagogue attack—framing protection from hate as a core governmental duty. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2023/feb/15/labour-out-of-ehrc-special-measures-after-progress-on-tackling-antisemitism?utm_source=openai))
- Professional human-rights pedigree prior to politics:
  - Decades as a human-rights barrister (Doughty Street Chambers; cases at the European Court of Human Rights; anti–death penalty work) and service as DPP issuing guidance that raised thresholds for speech prosecutions and protected public‑interest journalism—actions typically aligned with free expression rights. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/index.php/news/doughty-street-chambers-congratulates-sir-keir-starmer-victory-general-election?utm_source=openai))

Important counterpoints and how they affect the conclusion
- Stricter stance on elements of asylum law and ECHR interpretation in 2025:
  - In late 2025, Starmer signalled tightening the domestic application of certain ECHR articles (notably Articles 3 and 8) in deportation cases and announced plans to end automatic settlement and family-reunion rights for refugees, arguing deterrence and system integrity; these moves have drawn criticism from refugee and human-rights groups. However, he has simultaneously reaffirmed ECHR membership and the prohibition on returns to persecution (core non‑refoulement norms). This reflects a security/management tilt rather than rejection of the rights framework itself. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/oct/01/keir-starmer-human-rights-law-echr-nigel-farage-small-boat-crossings?utm_source=openai))
- Protest and public order:
  - Labour previously hesitated to promise wholesale repeal of recent protest restrictions, which civil-liberties advocates view as problematic. That said, the government’s strongest rights‑expanding legislative moves so far have been in labour rights rather than protest law. ([workersliberty.org](https://www.workersliberty.org/index.php/story/2023-06-06/re-establish-right-protest?utm_source=openai))

Synthesis
- Across career and government, Starmer has consistently anchored UK policy within the ECHR and human-rights law, enacted measures expanding certain domestic rights (notably workers’ rights), acted against antisemitism, and ended the Rwanda offshoring plan. These are substantive indicators that he values human rights.
- The 2025 asylum and interpretation shifts show a harder-edged approach to migration control that narrows the application of some rights in specific contexts, but they stop short of dismantling the rights framework he has repeatedly defended.

Reasoned conclusion
- Therefore, while reasonable people can criticise particular 2025 migration policies, the weight of evidence—professional history, ECHR commitments, concrete domestic rights legislation, and actions against discriminatory harms—supports the conclusion that Keir Starmer does value human rights, albeit with a pragmatic and sometimes restrictive approach in asylum policy rather than an across-the-board expansionist one. ([politics.co.uk](https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2024/11/04/we-will-never-withdraw-from-the-echr-keir-starmers-interpol-general-assembly-speech/?utm_source=openai))
